citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$
labels, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time
window $I_0$, and the collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Suppose the model presents its force map
through the time-independent potential
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),$$
where $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that
$F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain ([[post-cm02-interactions]],
clauses (iii) and (iv), [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\quad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\quad X:=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\quad V:=X',\quad P:=m_1x_1'+m_2x_2',\quad r:=x_1-x_2,$$
with $\lvert\cdot\rvert=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and dimensions as in [[def-cm01-units]]
($[M]=[\mu]=\mu$, $[X]=[r]=\ell$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$). Then:

1. **(Pair forces.)** On $J$ the evaluated forces are
   $$F_1\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r,\qquad F_2\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=+\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
   thus the model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of
   [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i) with
   $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ and the single pair force
   $F_{12}=-u'(\lvert r\rvert)r/\lvert r\rvert=-F_{21}$, which is central
   and antisymmetric in the sense of clause (ii).
2. **(Centre of mass.)** $P$ is constant on $J$ and $X$ is affine: for all
   $t,t_0\in J$, $X(t)=X(t_0)+(t-t_0)V$ with the constant
   $V=X'=M^{-1}P$.
3. **(Relative motion.)** $r$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, satisfies
   $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r(t)\rvert)}{\lvert r(t)\rvert}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   and is therefore a **central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$** in the
   sense of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]; its angular momentum vector
   $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+
   u(\lvert r\rvert)$ are the attached objects of that definition.
4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities
   $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$.
   Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with
   $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$
   on $J$, then
   $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$
   define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is
   $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently
   the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the
   model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$
   with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Adopt the following gravitational model and empirical premises for the
two-body part of this page, inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]] and the
central-force class of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (i).

**(i) The two-label gravitational model.** A model of the gravitational
branch is a model of class (i) of [[post-cm05-central-model]] with
$J_0=(0,\infty)$, $Q=\{x=(x_1,x_2):x_1\ne x_2\}$, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ in the
equation of motion, and the **gravitational pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2)=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}}{\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert},$$
where $G_{\mathrm N}>0$ is the **Newtonian constant of gravitation**, a
constant of dimension $\ell^{3}\mu^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ read in
$\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, and $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}>0$ are the
**gravitational coupling parameters** of the labels, primitive model data
distinct from the inertial masses $m_1,m_2$ ([[post-cm02-interactions]]
clause (v), [[def-cm01-units]]). The corresponding central pair potential of
class (i) is $u(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ with
$$\kappa:=G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}>0,\qquad\text{dimension } \mu\ell^{3}\tau^{-2};$$
it is of class $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$, the model has no external forces,
and coincident configurations are excluded. The force is attractive, and its
inverse-square form is an **adopted law** of this branch, not a consequence
of the equation of motion.

**(ii) The empirical mass identification.** For the quantitative
applications of this page, adopt in addition the identification
$$m_i^{g}=m_i\qquad(i=1,2)$$
of the gravitational coupling parameters with the inertial masses. This is an
**empirical assumption**, not part of clause (i) and not a consequence of the
equation of motion ([[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (vi)); it is the
content of the weak equivalence principle for these labels, and it is
adopted here only where a statement explicitly says so. When it is adopted,
$\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1m_2$, and every conclusion that uses it inherits its
empirical status; statements that never invoke clause (ii) remain conditional
on clause (i) alone, with $\kappa$ expressed through $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}$.

**(iii) The measured value of the constant.** When a model of this page is
used quantitatively, $G_{\mathrm N}$ may be **assigned** the CODATA 2022
recommended value
$$G_{\mathrm N}=6.674\,30(15)\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$
with standard uncertainty $0.000\,15\times10^{-11}$ in the same unit and
relative standard uncertainty $2.2\times10^{-5}$: a qualified empirical
premise, not a definition and not an exact value. The recommendation is a
least-squares value from 16 measurements whose mutual inconsistency led the
CODATA Task Group to expand its uncertainty by a factor of $3.9$, and the
2022 value agrees with the 2018 value because the input data were unchanged.
Any numerical conclusion that uses this assignment inherits the uncertainty
of $G_{\mathrm N}$ together with the uncertainties and conditions of the
other model data actually used; no such numerical conclusion is drawn by
this postulate itself.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The force equations in clause (i) define the
formal Newtonian point-particle model. The words **weak-field** and
**non-relativistic** specify when it is intended as an approximation to a
relativistic gravitational description. Let $c:=299792458\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
be the speed of light in vacuum, used here only as an external comparison
constant, not as a parameter in the Newtonian equations. For a configuration
$x=(x_1,x_2)\in Q$ with $\rho(x):=\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert>0$, define the
source potentials per unit gravitational coupling as scalar functions
$\Phi_1,\Phi_2:Q\to\mathbb R$ by
$$\Phi_1(x):=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}m_2^{g}}{\rho(x)},\qquad \Phi_2(x):=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}}{\rho(x)},$$
each of dimension $\ell^2\tau^{-2}$, and for a state velocity
$v=(v_1,v_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2$ define the dimensionless parameters
$$\epsilon_{\Phi}(x):=\frac{\max\{\lvert\Phi_1(x)\rvert,\lvert\Phi_2(x)\rvert\}}{c^2},\qquad \epsilon_v(v):=\frac{\lvert v_1-v_2\rvert^2}{c^2}.$$
For a motion $x:J\to Q$, a trajectory interval $\mathcal I\subseteq J$ and a dimensionless tolerance
$\eta\in(0,1)$ chosen small enough for the intended approximation, the
weak-field, slow-relative-motion regime on that segment means
$$\epsilon_{\Phi}(x(t))\le\eta\quad\text{and}\quad\epsilon_v(x'(t))\le\eta\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathcal I.$$
The choice of $\eta$ is application-specific; this model supplies no
relativistic correction estimate or error bound. When $G_{\mathrm N}$ is
assigned the value in clause (iii), these inequalities inherit its standard
uncertainty and any uncertainty in the other inputs; no regime assessment is
made here. The model treats the two
labels as point particles with fixed masses, ignores external bodies,
rotation, deformation, mass loss, radiation and any non-gravitational force,
and excludes coincident configurations. It is not asserted that any physical
system is exactly of this form; in particular, the identification of clause
(ii) is not a framework-wide identification, and the inverse-square law is
not derived from the balance laws of the framework.

**(v) Status.** Clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) are adopted assumptions of the
model and its empirical inputs; this item contains no proof and no
measurement of its own. The theorems of this page that invoke the model are
conditional on these clauses, and agreement of their predictions with
observations would test the combined model and apparatus assumptions rather
than prove them.

Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $U(\rho):=-\kappa/\rho$
(of class $C^2$), let $I$ be an interval with at least two points, and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant
angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$. Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]], let $I^\circ$ be the interior of $I$
(a nonempty interval with at least two points, or empty if $I$ is a singleton,
which is excluded), and put $W:=\theta(I^\circ)$, an interval. Then:

1. $\theta:I^\circ\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with inverse
   $\sigma:W\to I^\circ$ of class $C^1$, and the function
   $u:=1/(\rho\circ\sigma):W\to(0,\infty)$ is of class $C^2$;
2. on $W$, $u''+u=\mu\kappa/J^2$ (derivatives with respect to the variable of
   $W$);
3. the auxiliary identity $\rho'=-\dfrac{J}{\mu}\,u'\circ\theta$ holds on
   $I^\circ$;
4. the energy satisfies $E=\dfrac{J^2}{2\mu}\bigl((u')^2+u^2\bigr)-\kappa u$ on
   $W$, where $E$ is the constant energy of the trajectory.

Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant
angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$ and constant energy $E$
([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]), and let
$u:W\to(0,\infty)$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ be as in
[[thm-cm-kepler-binet-equation]], with $W=\theta(I^\circ)$. Write
$c:=\mu\kappa/J^2>0$ and $p:=1/c=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$. Then:

1. there are $e\ge0$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$ with
   $$u(\varphi)=c\bigl(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0)\bigr)\qquad(\varphi\in W),$$
   and for $t\in I^\circ$ accordingly
   $\rho(t)=p/\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_0)\bigr)$;
2. the energy and the eccentricity are related by
   $$E=\frac{\mu\kappa^2}{2J^2}\bigl(e^2-1\bigr);$$ consequently
   $E<0\iff e<1$, $E=0\iff e=1$ and $E>0\iff e>1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $p>0$ and
$0\le e<1$, and put
$$a:=\frac{p}{1-e^2}>0,\qquad b:=a\sqrt{1-e^2},\qquad \varrho(\varphi):=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\varphi}\quad(\varphi\in\mathbb R).$$

1. $\varrho$ is $C^1$, $2\pi$-periodic, and
   $\dfrac{p}{1+e}\le\varrho\le\dfrac{p}{1-e}$.
2. Let $Q(x,y):=(1-e^2)x^2+y^2+2pex-p^2$ and
   $E_{\rm ell}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:Q(x,y)\le0\}$. Then
   $E_{\rm ell}$ is Lebesgue measurable, and for the closed unit disc
   $\overline B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and $T(u,v):=(au-ae,bv)$ one has
   $E_{\rm ell}=T[\overline B]$; consequently
   $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\pi ab=\pi a^2\sqrt{1-e^2}$.
3. For every $\varphi$, the ray $\{s(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi):s>0\}$ meets
   $\partial E_{\rm ell}$ in the unique point
   $\varrho(\varphi)(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$; that point satisfies
   $Q=0$, and $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\varrho(\varphi)^2\,
   \mathrm d\varphi$.

Thus the conic $Q=0$ is the ellipse with centre $(-ae,0)$, semiaxes $a,b$,
its right focus at the origin, and enclosed area $\pi ab$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu>0$,
$\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum
$j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and constant energy $E<0$. Let $e\in[0,1)$,
$\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, $p=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$, $a=p/(1-e^2)$,
$b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$, and $\varrho(\varphi):=p/(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0))$
be the conic data of [[thm-cm-kepler-conic-and-eccentricity]], and let
$(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]. Then:

1. **(Completeness.)** $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory for
   $(\mu,U)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$; along it
   $\rho(t)\in[p/(1+e),\,p/(1-e)]$ for every $t$, and $\rho$ and $\rho'$ are
   bounded. Consequently every maximal central-force trajectory with these
   data has domain $\mathbb R$.
2. **(Periodicity.)** $\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a strictly increasing
   $C^1$ bijection with
   $\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1-e}{p}\Bigr)^2\le\theta'\le\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1+e}{p}\Bigr)^2$;
   if $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $T>0$ is determined by
   $\theta(t_0+T)=\theta(t_0)+2\pi$, then $r(t+T)=r(t)$ and
   $r'(t+T)=r'(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. **(Period value.)** With $r_{\max}:=p/(1-e)$ and $r_{\min}:=p/(1+e)$,
   $$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2}, \qquad T^2=\frac{4\pi^2\mu a^3}{\kappa}.$$

Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ whose angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ is a nonzero
constant vector ([[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]); write
$J:=|j|>0$. Let $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an oriented orthonormal triad with
$e_3=j/J$ ([[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]).

Then there are twice differentiable $\rho:I\to(0,\infty)$ and
$\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ with

$$r(t)=\rho(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta(t)\,e_2\bigr)\qquad(t\in I),$$

and for **every** such pair $(\rho,\theta)$:

1. $\rho(t)=|r(t)|$ for all $t$;
2. $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$ on $I$, so $\theta'>0$;
3. the effective-potential equation $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$
   holds on $I$, with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J=U+J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$
   ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]);
4. $E:=\frac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+U(|r|)$ equals
   $\frac12\mu\rho'^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)$ and is constant on $I$.

Call a triple $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ an **oriented
orthonormal triad** when $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ for all
$i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $e_1\times e_2=e_3$. Then:

1. **Existence.** For every $e_3\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|e_3|=1$ there are
   $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^3$ such that $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an oriented orthonormal
   triad.
2. **Dimension bound.** Every orthonormal list
   $f_1,\dots,f_m\in\mathbb R^3$ (pairwise orthogonal unit vectors) has
   $m\le3$; consequently, for every oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$
   and every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
   $$x=\langle x,e_1\rangle e_1+\langle x,e_2\rangle e_2+\langle x,e_3\rangle e_3, \qquad |x|^2=\langle x,e_1\rangle^2+\langle x,e_2\rangle^2+\langle x,e_3\rangle^2 .$$

Throughout, $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ are the Euclidean inner
product and norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), $\times$ is the cross
product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), and $s_1,s_2,s_3$ is the standard basis
of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [L1] the curve $r$ is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with constant nonzero angular momentum $Je_3$ and constant energy $E$, so the hypotheses of the inverse-square orbit theory [L2] are met and its polar representation and eccentricity-energy relation give the displayed formula and sign equivalences, since $\mu\kappa^{2}/(2J^{2})>0$. To verify the geometric description, for $e>0$ put $n_0:=\cos\theta_0e_1+\sin\theta_0e_2$ and $D:=\{y\in\Pi:\langle y,n_0\rangle=p/e\}$. For $t\in I^\circ$, set $\phi:=\theta(t)-\theta_0$. The formula and its positive denominator give $\rho(t)\cos\phi<p/e$ and $e\,d_\Pi(r(t),D)=e\bigl(p/e-\rho(t)\cos\phi\bigr)=p-e\rho(t)\cos\phi=\rho(t)=\lVert r(t)\rVert_2$, so $r(t)\in C(0,D,e)$ and the force centre is a focus. If $e=0$, the polar formula gives $\rho(t)=p$, so $r(t)$ lies on the stated circle.

Clause 2: differentiating $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ gives $\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)=\bigl(\kappa\rho-J^{2}/\mu\bigr)/\rho^{3}$, which vanishes exactly at $\rho_*$ and is negative for $\rho<\rho_*$ and positive for $\rho>\rho_*$; for $0<\rho<\rho'\le\rho_*$ the difference identity $$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho')-U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)=\frac{(\rho'-\rho)\bigl[2\mu\kappa\rho\rho'-J^{2}(\rho'+\rho)\bigr]}{2\mu\rho^{2}(\rho')^{2}}$$ has numerator at most $(\rho'-\rho)\bigl[2J^{2}\rho-J^{2}(\rho'+\rho)\bigr]=-J^{2}(\rho'-\rho)^{2}<0$, where the inequality uses $\rho\le\rho'$ and $\rho'\le\rho_*=J^{2}/(\mu\kappa)$; hence $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\rho_*]$ and $\rho_*$ is its unique minimum. Direct substitution gives $$-\frac{\kappa}{\rho_{\min}(E)}+\frac{J^{2}}{2\mu\rho_{\min}(E)^{2}}=E,$$ by multiplying by $\rho_{\min}^{2}$, clearing denominators with the definition of $\rho_{\min}$ and using $\bigl(\mu\kappa+\sqrt{\mu^{2}\kappa^{2}+2\mu EJ^{2}}\bigr)\bigl(-\mu\kappa+\sqrt{\mu^{2}\kappa^{2}+2\mu EJ^{2}}\bigr)=2\mu EJ^{2}$. Along the motion, the energy identity of [L2] gives $\tfrac12\mu(\rho')^{2}+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)=E$, so $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho(t))\le E=U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho_{\min}(E))$; if $\rho(t)\le\rho_*$ then strict decrease on $(0,\rho_*]$ forces $\rho(t)\ge\rho_{\min}(E)$, while if $\rho(t)>\rho_*$ then $\rho(t)>\rho_*\ge\rho_{\min}(E)$ because $\rho_{\min}(E)\le\rho_*$ (its defining denominator is at least $\mu\kappa$). Hence $\rho\ge\rho_{\min}(E)>0$ throughout.

Clause 3: assume $E<0$, so $e<1$ by step 1.1. Clause (a) is [L2] for the global relative trajectory $\bar r$. The affine curve $X$ has a unique affine extension $\bar X$ to $\mathbb R$ because $I$ has at least two points. Define $\bar x_1=\bar X+(m_2/M)\bar r$ and $\bar x_2=\bar X-(m_1/M)\bar r$ globally; the calculation in [L1] clause 4 shows that these satisfy the same time-independent equations. Their restriction to $I_0$ is a motion of the original model by that clause, and uniqueness follows from the unique relative and affine extensions. A global coordinate curve is a model motion on all of $\mathbb R$ only when the model time window is $I_0=\mathbb R$. Clause (b) is the ellipse clause of [L2], including $a=p/(1-e^{2})=-\kappa/(2E)$ and the bound on $\rho$. Clause (c): by [L1] and [L2], $\lvert x_1-X\rvert=\frac{m_2}{M}\lvert r\rvert=\frac{m_2}{M}\rho$ and $\lvert x_2-X\rvert=\frac{m_1}{M}\rho$, so substituting the conic of clause 1 gives the two displayed conic formulas; their semimajor axes are $p_j/(1-e^{2})=\frac{m_j}{M}a$ with the same eccentricity and the focus at the origin of $x_i-X$, which is the centre of mass.

Clause 4 and endpoints: [L2] gives $\rho=p/(1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0))$ on $I^\circ$. Equivalently, the continuous functions $t\mapsto\rho(t)(1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_0))$ and $t\mapsto p$ agree on $I^\circ$, so they agree on its closure in $I$, which is all of $I$; since $\rho(t)>0$ and $p>0$, this identity gives $1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_0)=p/\rho(t)>0$ and the conic formula also holds at every included endpoint of $I$. If $E=0$ then $e=1$ by step 1.1; the periapsis is $p/2=\rho_{\min}(0)$ by step 2.1. The conic locus is unbounded because $1+\cos\phi\downarrow0$ as $\phi\uparrow\pi$ through values below $\pi$. If $E>0$ then $e>1$; the periapsis is $\rho_{\min}(E)=p/(1+e)$ by step 2.1. With $\phi_*:=\arccos(-1/e)\in(0,\pi)$, the denominator $1+e\cos\phi$ is positive for $0\le\phi<\phi_*$ and tends to $0$ as $\phi\uparrow\phi_*$, so this conic locus is unbounded as well. These statements concern the full conic loci; no assertion is made that the actual time domain $I$ covers every point of either locus, or about asymptotic directions or scattering.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$
labels, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time
window $I_0$, and the collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Suppose the model presents its force map
through the time-independent potential
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),$$
where $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that
$F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain ([[post-cm02-interactions]],
clauses (iii) and (iv), [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\quad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\quad X:=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\quad V:=X',\quad P:=m_1x_1'+m_2x_2',\quad r:=x_1-x_2,$$
with $\lvert\cdot\rvert=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and dimensions as in [[def-cm01-units]]
($[M]=[\mu]=\mu$, $[X]=[r]=\ell$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$). Then:

1. **(Pair forces.)** On $J$ the evaluated forces are
   $$F_1\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r,\qquad F_2\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=+\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
   thus the model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of
   [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i) with
   $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ and the single pair force
   $F_{12}=-u'(\lvert r\rvert)r/\lvert r\rvert=-F_{21}$, which is central
   and antisymmetric in the sense of clause (ii).
2. **(Centre of mass.)** $P$ is constant on $J$ and $X$ is affine: for all
   $t,t_0\in J$, $X(t)=X(t_0)+(t-t_0)V$ with the constant
   $V=X'=M^{-1}P$.
3. **(Relative motion.)** $r$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, satisfies
   $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r(t)\rvert)}{\lvert r(t)\rvert}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   and is therefore a **central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$** in the
   sense of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]; its angular momentum vector
   $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+
   u(\lvert r\rvert)$ are the attached objects of that definition.
4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities
   $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$.
   Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with
   $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$
   on $J$, then
   $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$
   define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is
   $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently
   the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the
   model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$
   with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the
two-label gravitational model of [[post-cm05-gravity]] clause (i): inertial
masses $m_1,m_2>0$, $M=m_1+m_2$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/M$, gravitational
couplings $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}>0$, $\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}m_2^{g}>0$, and
the central pair potential $u(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $J_0=(0,\infty)$,
and model time window $I_0$. Let
$x:I\to Q$ be a motion on a time interval $I$ with nonempty interior, with
relative coordinate $r$, attached angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and
energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2-\kappa/\lvert r\rvert$
([[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]), and
suppose $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, for an oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.
Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data for $r$ and put
$$p:=\frac{J^{2}}{\mu\kappa},\qquad U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=-\frac{\kappa}{\rho}+\frac{J^{2}}{2\mu\rho^{2}},\qquad \rho_*:=\frac{J^{2}}{\mu\kappa}=p.$$
Then:

In the orbital plane $\Pi:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$, for a point
$F\in\Pi$, a line $D\subseteq\Pi$ with $F\notin D$, and $e>0$, define the
**focus-directrix conic of eccentricity $e$** to be
$$C(F,D,e):=\{y\in\Pi:\lVert y-F\rVert_2=e\,d_\Pi(y,D)\},\qquad d_\Pi(y,D):=\inf_{z\in D}\lVert y-z\rVert_2.$$
Here $F$ is a focus, $D$ is its directrix, and $e$ is the distance ratio in
the definition. The types $0<e<1$, $e=1$, and $e>1$ are called ellipse,
parabola, and hyperbola, respectively. The case $e=0$ is the circle of radius
$p$ centered at $F$, the circular ellipse with coincident foci at its centre.
In this item, an **unbounded conic** is a conic locus that is unbounded, not
an open subset of $\Pi$; the **periapsis distance** is the minimum distance
on the conic to its focus, and any point attaining it is a periapsis.

1. **(Conic and eccentricity.)** There are $e\ge0$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$
   with
   $$\rho=\frac{p}{1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)}$$
   on the interior of $I$, and the energy satisfies
   $E=\dfrac{\mu\kappa^{2}}{2J^{2}}\bigl(e^{2}-1\bigr)$; consequently
   $E<0\iff e<1$, $E=0\iff e=1$ and $E>0\iff e>1$. The relative trajectory
   lies on a focus-directrix conic with the force centre as focus when $e>0$: its
   directrix is $D=\{y\in\Pi:\langle y,n_0\rangle=p/e\}$, where
   $n_0:=\cos\theta_0e_1+\sin\theta_0e_2$. When $e=0$, the relative
   trajectory lies on the circle of radius $p$ centered at the force centre.
2. **(Centrifugal barrier.)** $\rho_*$ is the unique critical point of
   $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ in $(0,\infty)$ and the unique minimum, with
   $$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho_*)=-\frac{\mu\kappa^{2}}{2J^{2}};$$
   setting
   $$\rho_{\min}(E):=\frac{J^{2}}{\mu\kappa+\sqrt{\mu^{2}\kappa^{2}+2\mu EJ^{2}}}>0,$$
   one has $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho_{\min}(E))=E$ and
   $\rho(t)\ge\rho_{\min}(E)$ for every $t\in I$. In particular the relative
   motion never reaches the collision $r=0$, and
   $\rho_{\min}(E)=p/(1+e)$ is the periapsis distance of the conic of
   clause 1.
3. **(Elliptic case.)** If $E<0$, then $e<1$ and:
   (a) the relative trajectory extends uniquely to a central-force
   trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$. Together with
   the unique affine extension of $X$, this defines global coordinate curves
   $\bar x_1=\bar X+(m_2/M)\bar r$, $\bar x_2=\bar X-(m_1/M)\bar r$
   satisfying the same time-independent force equations; their restriction
   to $I_0$ is the unique extension of the model motion $x$. They are a
   model motion on all of $\mathbb R$ when $I_0=\mathbb R$. The relative
   motion is periodic, with
   $\theta(t+T)=\theta(t)+2\pi$ for one full angular revolution;
   (b) $r$ is an ellipse with focus at the force centre, semiaxes
   $$a=\frac{p}{1-e^{2}}=-\frac{\kappa}{2E},\qquad b=a\sqrt{1-e^{2}},$$
   and $p/(1+e)\le\rho\le p/(1-e)$;
   (c) each label's trajectory relative to the centre of mass is the conic
   of clause 1 scaled by $m_j/M$: with
   $p_1:=\frac{m_2}{M}p$, $p_2:=\frac{m_1}{M}p$ one has
   $$\lvert x_1-X\rvert=\frac{p_1}{1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)},\qquad \lvert x_2-X\rvert=\frac{p_2}{1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)},$$
   so both labels trace ellipses with the centre of mass at a focus, the
   same eccentricity $e$ and semimajor axes $a_1=\frac{m_2}{M}a$,
   $a_2=\frac{m_1}{M}a$.
4. **(Parabolic and hyperbolic cases on the domain of the motion.)** If
   $E=0$, then $e=1$ and
   $\rho=p/\bigl(1+\cos(\theta-\theta_0)\bigr)$ with periapsis
   $\rho_{\min}(0)=p/2$. If $E>0$, then $e>1$ and the formula of clause 1
   holds at every $t$ with $1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)>0$, with periapsis
   $\rho_{\min}(E)=p/(1+e)$. In both cases $e\ge1$ and the corresponding
   conic locus is unbounded;
   the extent of the trajectory, its asymptotes and its scattering
   interpretation are **not** claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu>0$,
$\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum
$j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and constant energy $E<0$. Let $e\in[0,1)$,
$\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, $p=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$, $a=p/(1-e^2)$,
$b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$, and $\varrho(\varphi):=p/(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0))$
be the conic data of [[thm-cm-kepler-conic-and-eccentricity]], and let
$(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]. Then:

1. **(Completeness.)** $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory for
   $(\mu,U)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$; along it
   $\rho(t)\in[p/(1+e),\,p/(1-e)]$ for every $t$, and $\rho$ and $\rho'$ are
   bounded. Consequently every maximal central-force trajectory with these
   data has domain $\mathbb R$.
2. **(Periodicity.)** $\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a strictly increasing
   $C^1$ bijection with
   $\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1-e}{p}\Bigr)^2\le\theta'\le\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1+e}{p}\Bigr)^2$;
   if $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $T>0$ is determined by
   $\theta(t_0+T)=\theta(t_0)+2\pi$, then $r(t+T)=r(t)$ and
   $r'(t+T)=r'(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. **(Period value.)** With $r_{\max}:=p/(1-e)$ and $r_{\min}:=p/(1+e)$,
   $$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2}, \qquad T^2=\frac{4\pi^2\mu a^3}{\kappa}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $p>0$ and
$0\le e<1$, and put
$$a:=\frac{p}{1-e^2}>0,\qquad b:=a\sqrt{1-e^2},\qquad \varrho(\varphi):=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\varphi}\quad(\varphi\in\mathbb R).$$

1. $\varrho$ is $C^1$, $2\pi$-periodic, and
   $\dfrac{p}{1+e}\le\varrho\le\dfrac{p}{1-e}$.
2. Let $Q(x,y):=(1-e^2)x^2+y^2+2pex-p^2$ and
   $E_{\rm ell}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:Q(x,y)\le0\}$. Then
   $E_{\rm ell}$ is Lebesgue measurable, and for the closed unit disc
   $\overline B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and $T(u,v):=(au-ae,bv)$ one has
   $E_{\rm ell}=T[\overline B]$; consequently
   $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\pi ab=\pi a^2\sqrt{1-e^2}$.
3. For every $\varphi$, the ray $\{s(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi):s>0\}$ meets
   $\partial E_{\rm ell}$ in the unique point
   $\varrho(\varphi)(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$; that point satisfies
   $Q=0$, and $\lambda_2(E_{\rm ell})=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\varrho(\varphi)^2\,
   \mathrm d\varphi$.

Thus the conic $Q=0$ is the ellipse with centre $(-ae,0)$, semiaxes $a,b$,
its right focus at the origin, and enclosed area $\pi ab$.

Adopt the central-force model of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (i): masses
$m_1,m_2>0$, $M=m_1+m_2$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/M$, static central pair
potential $u\in C^2(J_0)$, and a motion $x:I\to Q$ on a time interval $I$ with
nonempty interior; let $X$ be its centre of mass, $r=x_1-x_2$ its relative
coordinate, and $j:=\mu\,r\times r'$ the attached angular-momentum vector
([[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]). Then:

1. **(Plane.)** $j$ is constant on $I$, and $\langle r(t),j\rangle=0$ and
   $\langle r'(t),j\rangle=0$ for every $t\in I$; if $j\ne0$, the relative
   trajectory is contained in the fixed plane
   $\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\langle y,j\rangle=0\}$ through the force centre with
   normal $j$.
2. **(Areal velocity.)** Suppose $j\ne0$ and write $J:=\lvert j\rvert>0$.
   Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data for $r$ in an oriented orthonormal triad
   with $e_3=j/J$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Then
   $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu>0$, and the **areal-velocity vector**
   $$\omega(t):=\tfrac12\,r(t)\times r'(t)$$
   is constant and equal to $j/(2\mu)$; in particular
   $\lvert\omega(t)\rvert=J/(2\mu)$ for all $t$.
3. **(Equal areas in equal times.)** With $(\rho,\theta)$ as in clause 2 and
   $t_0\in I$, the **swept-area function**
   $$A(t):=\frac12\int_{t_0}^{t}\rho(s)^2\theta'(s)\,ds\qquad(t\in I)$$
   is of class $C^1$ with $A'\equiv J/(2\mu)$; hence for all
   $t_0<t_1$ in $I$ one has $A(t_1)-A(t_0)=(t_1-t_0)J/(2\mu)$.
4. **(Both labels about the centre of mass.)** With $j\ne0$ as in clause 2,
   for every $t\in I$,
   $$\tfrac12\bigl(x_1(t)-X(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(x_1(t)-X(t)\bigr)'=\Bigl(\frac{m_2}{M}\Bigr)^{2}\omega(t),\qquad \tfrac12\bigl(x_2(t)-X(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(x_2(t)-X(t)\bigr)'=\Bigl(\frac{m_1}{M}\Bigr)^{2}\omega(t),$$
   so each label's areal-velocity vector about the centre of mass is
   constant; their magnitudes are in the ratio $(m_2/m_1)^2$.

Adopt the following gravitational model and empirical premises for the
two-body part of this page, inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]] and the
central-force class of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (i).

**(i) The two-label gravitational model.** A model of the gravitational
branch is a model of class (i) of [[post-cm05-central-model]] with
$J_0=(0,\infty)$, $Q=\{x=(x_1,x_2):x_1\ne x_2\}$, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ in the
equation of motion, and the **gravitational pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2)=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}}{\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert},$$
where $G_{\mathrm N}>0$ is the **Newtonian constant of gravitation**, a
constant of dimension $\ell^{3}\mu^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ read in
$\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, and $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}>0$ are the
**gravitational coupling parameters** of the labels, primitive model data
distinct from the inertial masses $m_1,m_2$ ([[post-cm02-interactions]]
clause (v), [[def-cm01-units]]). The corresponding central pair potential of
class (i) is $u(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ with
$$\kappa:=G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}>0,\qquad\text{dimension } \mu\ell^{3}\tau^{-2};$$
it is of class $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$, the model has no external forces,
and coincident configurations are excluded. The force is attractive, and its
inverse-square form is an **adopted law** of this branch, not a consequence
of the equation of motion.

**(ii) The empirical mass identification.** For the quantitative
applications of this page, adopt in addition the identification
$$m_i^{g}=m_i\qquad(i=1,2)$$
of the gravitational coupling parameters with the inertial masses. This is an
**empirical assumption**, not part of clause (i) and not a consequence of the
equation of motion ([[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (vi)); it is the
content of the weak equivalence principle for these labels, and it is
adopted here only where a statement explicitly says so. When it is adopted,
$\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1m_2$, and every conclusion that uses it inherits its
empirical status; statements that never invoke clause (ii) remain conditional
on clause (i) alone, with $\kappa$ expressed through $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}$.

**(iii) The measured value of the constant.** When a model of this page is
used quantitatively, $G_{\mathrm N}$ may be **assigned** the CODATA 2022
recommended value
$$G_{\mathrm N}=6.674\,30(15)\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$
with standard uncertainty $0.000\,15\times10^{-11}$ in the same unit and
relative standard uncertainty $2.2\times10^{-5}$: a qualified empirical
premise, not a definition and not an exact value. The recommendation is a
least-squares value from 16 measurements whose mutual inconsistency led the
CODATA Task Group to expand its uncertainty by a factor of $3.9$, and the
2022 value agrees with the 2018 value because the input data were unchanged.
Any numerical conclusion that uses this assignment inherits the uncertainty
of $G_{\mathrm N}$ together with the uncertainties and conditions of the
other model data actually used; no such numerical conclusion is drawn by
this postulate itself.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The force equations in clause (i) define the
formal Newtonian point-particle model. The words **weak-field** and
**non-relativistic** specify when it is intended as an approximation to a
relativistic gravitational description. Let $c:=299792458\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
be the speed of light in vacuum, used here only as an external comparison
constant, not as a parameter in the Newtonian equations. For a configuration
$x=(x_1,x_2)\in Q$ with $\rho(x):=\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert>0$, define the
source potentials per unit gravitational coupling as scalar functions
$\Phi_1,\Phi_2:Q\to\mathbb R$ by
$$\Phi_1(x):=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}m_2^{g}}{\rho(x)},\qquad \Phi_2(x):=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}}{\rho(x)},$$
each of dimension $\ell^2\tau^{-2}$, and for a state velocity
$v=(v_1,v_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2$ define the dimensionless parameters
$$\epsilon_{\Phi}(x):=\frac{\max\{\lvert\Phi_1(x)\rvert,\lvert\Phi_2(x)\rvert\}}{c^2},\qquad \epsilon_v(v):=\frac{\lvert v_1-v_2\rvert^2}{c^2}.$$
For a motion $x:J\to Q$, a trajectory interval $\mathcal I\subseteq J$ and a dimensionless tolerance
$\eta\in(0,1)$ chosen small enough for the intended approximation, the
weak-field, slow-relative-motion regime on that segment means
$$\epsilon_{\Phi}(x(t))\le\eta\quad\text{and}\quad\epsilon_v(x'(t))\le\eta\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathcal I.$$
The choice of $\eta$ is application-specific; this model supplies no
relativistic correction estimate or error bound. When $G_{\mathrm N}$ is
assigned the value in clause (iii), these inequalities inherit its standard
uncertainty and any uncertainty in the other inputs; no regime assessment is
made here. The model treats the two
labels as point particles with fixed masses, ignores external bodies,
rotation, deformation, mass loss, radiation and any non-gravitational force,
and excludes coincident configurations. It is not asserted that any physical
system is exactly of this form; in particular, the identification of clause
(ii) is not a framework-wide identification, and the inverse-square law is
not derived from the balance laws of the framework.

**(v) Status.** Clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) are adopted assumptions of the
model and its empirical inputs; this item contains no proof and no
measurement of its own. The theorems of this page that invoke the model are
conditional on these clauses, and agreement of their predictions with
observations would test the combined model and apparatus assumptions rather
than prove them.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [L1] the relative trajectory meets the hypotheses of [L2] with $E<0$, and [L2] supplies the unique extension to $\mathbb R$, the periodicity with $T$ determined by one full revolution of $\theta$, and the two displayed period formulas; substituting $a=p/(1-e^{2})$ and $p=J^{2}/(\mu\kappa)$ into $T=2\pi\mu ab/J$ and $T=2\pi\sqrt{\mu/\kappa}\,a^{3/2}$ is exactly [L2].

Clause 2: substituting $\mu=m_1m_2/M$ and $\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}m_2^{g}$ from [L4] into $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}\mu a^{3}/\kappa$ gives $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}a^{3}m_1m_2/\bigl(MG_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}m_2^{g}\bigr)$; if additionally $m_i^{g}=m_i$, the numerator and denominator simplify by $m_1m_2$ to $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}a^{3}/(G_{\mathrm N}M)$.

Clause 3: use the global coordinate extension of [L2], which restricts to a model motion on $I_0$. By [L1], $x_i-X=\pm\frac{m_j}{M}r$, and $r$, hence $x_i-X$, is $T$-periodic by step 1.1; also $X(t+T)-X(t)=VT$ because $X$ is affine with constant derivative $V$, so $x_i(t+T)-x_i(t)=VT+\bigl(x_i(t+T)-X(t+T)\bigr)-\bigl(x_i(t)-X(t)\bigr)=VT$. If $V=0$, this proves that both absolute motions are $T$-periodic. Conversely, suppose either absolute motion $x_i$ has any positive period $S$. For every positive integer $n$, periodicity and the affine motion of $X$ give $0=x_i(t+nS)-x_i(t)=nVS\pm\frac{m_j}{M}\bigl(r(t+nS)-r(t)\bigr)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$. By the conic bound in [L2], $\lVert r(t)\rVert_2\le p/(1-e)$ for all $t$, so $nS\lVert V\rVert_2\le2(m_j/M)p/(1-e)$ for every $n$. Since the right side is fixed and $S>0$, this forces $V=0$. Thus either label has an absolute period only if $V=0$, and when $V=0$ both are periodic.

Clause 4: by [L2] the relative motion extends to $\mathbb R$; applying the relative areal-rate identity of [L3] to the global central-force trajectory, its swept-area function has derivative $J/(2\mu)$, so the area swept over one period is $JT/(2\mu)$. Since $\theta:[t_0,t_0+T]\to[\theta(t_0),\theta(t_0)+2\pi]$ is a strictly increasing $C^1$ bijection with $\theta'=\rho^{-2}\mu^{-1}J$ on the extension, the substitution rule gives $$A(t_0+T)-A(t_0)=\frac12\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T}\rho^{2}\theta'=\frac12\int_{\theta(t_0)}^{\theta(t_0)+2\pi}\varrho(\varphi)^{2}\,\mathrm d\varphi=\frac12\int_{0}^{2\pi}\varrho(\varphi)^{2}\,\mathrm d\varphi=\pi ab$$ by the $2\pi$-periodicity of $\varrho$ and [L2]; combining with $A(t_0+T)-A(t_0)=JT/(2\mu)$ gives $T=2\pi\mu ab/J$.
